name: Sagittal split jaw width reduction

card.summary: A proposed jaw-surgery approach that splits the jawbone to change its width, discussed in hardmaxxing circles as a route to a narrower lower face.
card.note: Sagittal split osteotomy is established for jaw advancement/setback; use for width reduction is a community concept.

quick.overview:
Bilateral sagittal split osteotomy (BSSO) is an established orthognathic operation in which the lower jaw is cut and split on each side so it can be moved forward or back. Hardmaxxing discussions extend the idea to splitting jawbone to reduce overall width.

The established surgery is used for bite and jaw-position problems and often also changes facial balance and appearance.
quick.how: In standard BSSO the surgeon cuts the jawbone on each side, splits it, repositions the lower jaw and fixes it with plates and screws. Healing takes weeks to months.
quick.risks: Reported complications include swelling, infection, bleeding and injury to the inferior alveolar nerve causing numbness, usually temporary; relapse is also studied.

lead: Sagittal split jaw width reduction is a looksmaxxing-community term for using the sagittal split technique to alter lower-jaw width. The underlying operation, bilateral sagittal split osteotomy (BSSO), is a mainstream orthognathic procedure popularised by Hugo Obwegeser to correct mandibular retrusion and prognathism.[1]

In BSSO the surgeon cuts and splits the jaw bone on each side, moves the lower jaw forward or back, and fixes it with titanium plates and screws.[1] It is used mainly for bite and jaw-position problems, and also for facial balance.[1] Published literature focuses on advancement, setback and stability rather than a dedicated width-reduction procedure.[2]

chain: Lower jaw bone cut and repositioned
angle.text: Established BSSO changes jaw position, which can noticeably change the face. Community proponents discuss extending the split technique to narrow jaw width.

paras: Orthognathic surgery corrects dentofacial deformities that orthodontics cannot alone, and usually produces a noticeable change in the face.[1] Planning software can predict post-operative shape.[1]

Complications include bleeding, swelling and infection (up to 7 percent reported), and inferior alveolar nerve injury causing numbness that usually recovers within about three months and is rarely permanent.[1] Studies also review post-surgical stability and relapse after sagittal osteotomy.[2][3]

Trials of BSSO examine nerve recovery, fixation and stability, including randomised trials of low-level laser therapy and selegiline for neurosensory recovery.[4][5] No studies found specifically on sagittal split for jaw width reduction.
